VIDEO.title: The HIDDEN Meaning Behind Jesus Cursing the Fig Tree
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 21:1-22 · Episode 41 (#44 of 58 in the playlist)
hand: Hosanna to the Son of David
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 21:1-22. Near Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sends two disciples for a donkey and her colt, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. Crowds spread garments and branches and cry, 'Hosanna to the Son of David.' He enters the temple, drives out the buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers' tables, and quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. He heals the blind and lame, and when the leaders object to the children's praise He quotes Psalm 8:2. The next morning He curses a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and it withers; then He teaches about faith that moves 'this mountain.'

Bethphage means 'house of unripe figs,' which sets up the fig tree. It is the Sunday before Passover (John 12). Two crowds meet: pilgrims with Him from Galilee and Jerusalemites coming out with palm branches. Zechariah's prophecy, written about five centuries earlier, is acted out on purpose.

Entering from the east, from the Mount of Olives, recalls Zechariah 14:4. The cries come from Psalm 118, sung at the Feast of Booths, and Hosanna means 'save, please.' In the temple Jesus judges the priestly leaders, the shepherds of Isaiah 56:10-11, and welcomes the blind and lame.

The fig tree is a picture of the leaders. Jeremiah 8:13 pronounces judgment on a fruitless people: no figs on the fig tree, the leaf will wither. And 'this mountain' that can be cast into the sea is likely the Temple Mount, right in front of them.
The lesson: Jesus expects His disciples to be a kingdom of priests that possess unwavering faith in Him and continue to intercede on behalf of God's people (Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:5).
QUOTES: Jesus expects his disciples to be a kingdom of priests that possess unwavering faith in him and continue to intercede on behalf of God's people.
Matthew makes this clear that this is to fulfill Zechariah 9:9.
So, the fig tree actually represented Israel's leaders.
The Lord rebukes Israel's corrupt leaders as shepherds who have no understanding.

method.h: Read the prophets the scene acts out
method.p: Matthew 21 is full of acted prophecy. When Jesus does something odd, look for the Old Testament text He is performing: Zechariah 9, Psalm 118, Isaiah 56, Jeremiah 7 and 8.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Behold your King is coming to you, / Lowly, and mounted on a donkey,
It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a robbers’ den.
and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

left.text: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! / Make a loud shout, O daughter of Jerusalem! / Behold, your king is coming to you; / He is righteous and endowed with salvation, / Lowly and mounted on a donkey, / Even on a colt, the foal of a pack animal.

right.text: and brought the donkey and the colt, and laid their garments on them; and He sat on the garments.

lines.text: Zechariah saw his visions around 500 BC, while the Jews waited to return after Babylon. Matthew makes clear that Jesus fulfills Zechariah 9:9 on purpose.
Only Matthew mentions two animals. One commentator the video cites suggests the mother came along to keep the young colt calm; Mark 11:2 says no one had ever sat on it.
Bethphage, 'house of unripe figs,' sits on the Mount of Olives, east of the city across the Kidron.

left.text: And the crowds going ahead of Him, and those who followed, were crying out, saying, / “Hosanna to the Son of David; / Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord; / Hosanna in the highest!”

right.text: took the branches of the palm trees and went out to meet Him, and began to shout, “Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel.”

lines.text: It is the Sunday before Passover. One crowd comes with Him from Galilee; another comes out of Jerusalem to meet Him with palm branches.
The cries come from Psalm 118:26 and Psalm 148:1, psalms sung at the Feast of Booths. Hosanna means 'save, please.'
The Mishnah describes the lulav being waved at Psalm 118:25, 'Lord, please save us' (Mishnah Sukkah 3:9), and the altar being circled each day with the same words (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5).

src.text: And in that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, which is in front of Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split in its middle from east to west by a very large valley so that half of the mountain will move toward the north and the other half toward the south.

lines.text: Jesus comes down from the Mount of Olives into the city from the east, where Zechariah pictures Yahweh's feet standing.
The video suggests Pilate may have been entering from the west at the same feast with a military parade; that is a suggestion, not something the Gospels say.
The video links the eastern gate to the Beautiful Gate of Acts 3:2 and to later hopes that Messiah will enter there.

src.text: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all those who were buying and selling in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who were selling doves. And He *said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a robbers’ den.”

lines.text: This is not the cleansing of John 2:13-17; the video sees two cleansings, one at the start and one at the end of His ministry.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. The sellers were in the outer court, the place set aside for the nations to pray.
Pilgrims needed approved animals and coins for temple payments; the dispute is over where and how the trade was run, inside the sacred precinct.

left.text: Even those I will bring to My holy mountain / And make them glad in My house of prayer. / Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar; / For My house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples.”

right.text: His watchmen are blind; / All of them know nothing. / All of them are mute dogs unable to bark, / Dreamers lying down, who love to slumber;

lines.text: Read on in Isaiah 56: the watchmen are blind, and the shepherds turn 'each one to his greedy gain' (56:11). Jesus' quotation points at the leaders.
Salvation was meant to be free: 'come, buy wine and milk / Without money' (Isaiah 55:1), and 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink' (John 7:37).

The Talmud preserves a lament over priestly families: 'Woe is me due to the High Priests of the house of Ḥanin; woe is me due to their whispers and the rumors they spread' (Talmud Pesachim 57a). The house of Ḥanin is generally identified with Annas.

left.text: and said to Him, “Do You hear what these children are saying?” And Jesus *said to them, “Yes; have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have prepared praise for Yourself’?”

right.text: From the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have established strength / Because of Your adversaries, / To make the enemy and the revengeful cease.

lines.text: The blind and lame come and are healed; the leaders are indignant. Jesus answers with Psalm 8:2 and leaves the rest of the verse unspoken: 'because of Your adversaries.'
The Mishnah says one may not enter the Temple Mount with a staff, shoes or money belt, and may not make it a shortcut (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5), a picture of the reverence the place was meant to have.

src.text: And seeing a lone fig tree by the road, He came to it and found nothing on it except leaves only; and He *said to it, “No longer shall there ever be any fruit from you.” And at once the fig tree withered.

lines.text: Jesus is not angry at a tree. The fig tree stands for Israel, and more exactly for Israel's leaders: a show of leaves, no fruit.
Mark 11:12-21 splits the story around the temple scene, cursing on one day and finding it withered the next, which makes the link plain.

left.text: Has this house, which is called by My name, become a robbers’ den in your sight? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” declares Yahweh.

right.text: “I will surely gather them up,” declares Yahweh; / “There will be no grapes on the vine / And no figs on the fig tree, / And the leaf will wither; / And what I have given them will pass away.”’”

lines.text: Jesus quoted Jeremiah 7:11 in the temple. A few verses on, God warns He will cast them out of His sight (7:15), and in 8:13 there are no figs on the fig tree and the leaf withers.
Anyone who knew the passage would hear it: the temple scene and the fig tree are one message.

src.text: And Jesus answered and said to them, “Truly I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it will happen. And all things you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

lines.text: 'This mountain' is most likely the Temple Mount, right in front of them, as 17:20 pointed to a mountain nearby.
So the promise is not a magic trick. A faithful, praying people can see corrupt power removed.
That is priestly work: 'you also, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house for a holy priesthood' (1 Peter 2:5).

TERMS.def: From Hebrew for save, please (Psalm 118:25); a cry of praise and plea.
'House of unripe figs,' a village on the Mount of Olives.
Sukkot, the autumn feast when Psalm 118 was sung with waving branches.
The outer court of the temple, open to the nations.
Traders who exchanged coins for those accepted for temple payments.
God's calling for His people to intercede for others (Exodus 19:6).

WORDS.gloss: To doubt, waver. Look up: BDAG, διακρίνω.

BACKGROUND.p: Psalm 118 belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113-118), sung at the pilgrim feasts. At the Feast of Booths the Mishnah says they waved the lulav at 'Lord, please save us' (Mishnah Sukkah 3:9) and each day circled the altar saying, 'Lord, please save us. Lord, please grant us success' (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5).

In Jesus' day the high priesthood was appointed by Herod and then by Rome, and a few families held it. The Talmud records: 'The power of these households stemmed from the fact that the fathers were High Priests, and their sons were the Temple treasurers' (Talmud Pesachim 57a).

The gate in the eastern wall today, the Golden Gate (Gate of Mercy), was built long after Jesus and has been sealed for centuries. Jewish and later traditions connect the eastern approach with the Messiah, drawing on Zechariah 14:4 and Ezekiel 44:1-3.

DEBATES.p: John places a temple cleansing at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2), the other Gospels at the end. Many, with Chrysostom, see two events; others think John placed one event early for theological reasons.

DEBATES.h: Why curse a tree out of season?
DEBATES.p: Mark notes 'it was not the season for figs' (Mark 11:13). Most read the act as an enacted parable of judgment, like the prophets' sign-acts, rather than a fit of hunger.
Some take 'this mountain' as a general picture of the impossible; others, like the video, as the Temple Mount or the Mount of Olives in view.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: In 21:15 the LSB says 'the chief priests and the scribes' became indignant; the video calls them Pharisees there.
The video names the high-priestly line 'Zadok or Zedekiah'; Zedekiah was Judah's last king, and the high priests of Jesus' day were appointed by Herod and by Rome rather than following Zadok's line.
Acts 3:2 names a temple gate 'Beautiful' but does not say where it was; many place it on the inner courts rather than the outer eastern wall.

The claims that Josephus says the chief priests owned the money exchange, and that waving palm fronds was punishable by crucifixion, are given without a source. The closest text found for the first is the Talmud's lament over the priestly houses (Pesachim 57a).
Mark 11:17 quotes Isaiah 56:7 with 'for all the nations'; the LSB of Isaiah 56:7 reads 'for all the peoples.'
Caption spellings: 'Bethpage' is Bethphage and 'Hosana' is Hosanna.

QUESTIONS: Why did Jesus choose a donkey and colt rather than a horse or chariot?
What do the two crowds, from Galilee and from Jerusalem, suggest about the city's mood?
How does the rest of Isaiah 56 sharpen what Jesus said in the temple?
What does the fig tree with 'leaves only' look like in a church or a life today?
How is faith that 'moves this mountain' connected to praying for others?
Who could you intercede for this week as part of a kingdom of priests?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: Jesus expects His disciples to be a kingdom of priests that possess unwavering faith in Him and continue to intercede on behalf of God's people. The fig tree shows what happens to leaders who look fruitful but bear none. The corrupt priests were meant to draw near and intercede for God's people; now Jesus' disciples are to be His intercessors. The idea runs from Exodus 19:6 through 2 Chronicles 30:27 and Isaiah 61:6 to 1 Peter 2:5. This is not a license to ask for whatever we want, but a call to faithful, priestly prayer.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): write down three people or places you will pray for daily this week, and one 'leaves only' area of your own life where you want real fruit.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 21:1-22. Near Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sends two disciples for a donkey and her colt, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. Crowds spread garments and branches and cry, 'Hosanna to the Son of David.' He enters the temple, drives out the buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers' tables, and quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. He heals the blind and lame, and when the leaders object to the children's praise He quotes Psalm 8:2. The next morning He curses a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and it withers; then He teaches about faith that moves 'this mountain.'
- Bethphage means 'house of unripe figs,' which sets up the fig tree. It is the Sunday before Passover (John 12). Two crowds meet: pilgrims with Him from Galilee and Jerusalemites coming out with palm branches. Zechariah's prophecy, written about five centuries earlier, is acted out on purpose.
- Entering from the east, from the Mount of Olives, recalls Zechariah 14:4. The cries come from Psalm 118, sung at the Feast of Booths, and Hosanna means 'save, please.' In the temple Jesus judges the priestly leaders, the shepherds of Isaiah 56:10-11, and welcomes the blind and lame.
- The fig tree is a picture of the leaders. Jeremiah 8:13 pronounces judgment on a fruitless people: no figs on the fig tree, the leaf will wither. And 'this mountain' that can be cast into the sea is likely the Temple Mount, right in front of them.
- The lesson: Jesus expects His disciples to be a kingdom of priests that possess unwavering faith in Him and continue to intercede on behalf of God's people (Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:5).

Matthew 21 is full of acted prophecy. When Jesus does something odd, look for the Old Testament text He is performing: Zechariah 9, Psalm 118, Isaiah 56, Jeremiah 7 and 8.

## A house of prayer
1. Matthew 21:12-13: A robbers' den
   Judgment Matthew 21:12-13: "And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all those who were buying and selling in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who were selling doves. And He *said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you are making it a robbers’ den.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+21:12-13
   (video) This is not the cleansing of John 2:13-17; the video sees two cleansings, one at the start and one at the end of His ministry. (John 2:13-17)
   (video) Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. The sellers were in the outer court, the place set aside for the nations to pray.
   [Background] Pilgrims needed approved animals and coins for temple payments; the dispute is over where and how the trade was run, inside the sacred precinct.
2. Isaiah 56:7, 10-11: Blind watchmen
   Isaiah (Isaiah 56:7, LSB): "Even those I will bring to My holy mountain / And make them glad in My house of prayer. / Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be acceptable on My altar; / For My house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples.”"
   Isaiah (Isaiah 56:10, LSB): "His watchmen are blind; / All of them know nothing. / All of them are mute dogs unable to bark, / Dreamers lying down, who love to slumber;"
   (video) Read on in Isaiah 56: the watchmen are blind, and the shepherds turn 'each one to his greedy gain' (56:11). Jesus' quotation points at the leaders. (Isaiah 56:11)
   (video) Salvation was meant to be free: 'come, buy wine and milk / Without money' (Isaiah 55:1), and 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink' (John 7:37). (Isaiah 55:1; John 7:37-38)
   [Background] The Talmud preserves a lament over priestly families: 'Woe is me due to the High Priests of the house of Ḥanin; woe is me due to their whispers and the rumors they spread' (Talmud Pesachim 57a). The house of Ḥanin is generally identified with Annas.
3. Matthew 21:14-16; Psalm 8:2: Praise from children
   Jesus (Matthew 21:16, LSB): "and said to Him, “Do You hear what these children are saying?” And Jesus *said to them, “Yes; have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have prepared praise for Yourself’?”"
   David (Psalm 8:2, LSB): "From the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have established strength / Because of Your adversaries, / To make the enemy and the revengeful cease."
   (video) The blind and lame come and are healed; the leaders are indignant. Jesus answers with Psalm 8:2 and leaves the rest of the verse unspoken: 'because of Your adversaries.'
   [Background] The Mishnah says one may not enter the Temple Mount with a staff, shoes or money belt, and may not make it a shortcut (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5), a picture of the reverence the place was meant to have.

## The fig tree and the mountain
1. Matthew 21:18-20: Leaves only
   Acted parable Matthew 21:19: "And seeing a lone fig tree by the road, He came to it and found nothing on it except leaves only; and He *said to it, “No longer shall there ever be any fruit from you.” And at once the fig tree withered." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+21:19
   (video) Jesus is not angry at a tree. The fig tree stands for Israel, and more exactly for Israel's leaders: a show of leaves, no fruit.
   [Background] Mark 11:12-21 splits the story around the temple scene, cursing on one day and finding it withered the next, which makes the link plain. (Mark 11:12-21)
2. Jeremiah 7:11; 8:13: Jeremiah's fig tree
   Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:11, LSB): "Has this house, which is called by My name, become a robbers’ den in your sight? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” declares Yahweh."
   Jeremiah (Jeremiah 8:13, LSB): "“I will surely gather them up,” declares Yahweh; / “There will be no grapes on the vine / And no figs on the fig tree, / And the leaf will wither; / And what I have given them will pass away.”’”"
   (video) Jesus quoted Jeremiah 7:11 in the temple. A few verses on, God warns He will cast them out of His sight (7:15), and in 8:13 there are no figs on the fig tree and the leaf withers. (Jeremiah 7:15)
   (video) Anyone who knew the passage would hear it: the temple scene and the fig tree are one message.
3. Matthew 21:21-22: This mountain
   Faith Matthew 21:21-22: "And Jesus answered and said to them, “Truly I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it will happen. And all things you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+21:21-22
   (video) 'This mountain' is most likely the Temple Mount, right in front of them, as 17:20 pointed to a mountain nearby.
   (video) So the promise is not a magic trick. A faithful, praying people can see corrupt power removed.
   (video) That is priestly work: 'you also, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house for a holy priesthood' (1 Peter 2:5).

## Key people
- The two disciples: Sent for the donkey and colt. [Background] Unnamed in all three Gospels.
- The crowds: Two crowds: pilgrims from Galilee and Jerusalemites with palm branches. [Background] John says the crowd came out because they had heard He raised Lazarus (John 12:17-18).
- The money changers and dove sellers: Driven out; their tables overturned. [Background] Pilgrims bought doves for offerings, and paid temple dues in approved coin.
- The blind and the lame: Come to Him in the temple and are healed. [Background] Compare 2 Samuel 5:8, where the blind and lame are kept out.
- The children: Shout 'Hosanna to the Son of David' in the temple. [Background] Jesus answers with Psalm 8:2.
- The chief priests and scribes: Indignant at the praise; represented by the fig tree. [Background] The priestly families controlled the temple; Annas's house is lamented in Talmud Pesachim 57a.

## Places [Background]
- Bethany (named in the video): He spent the night there (21:17).
- Bethphage (named in the video): 'Came to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives' (21:1).
- Temple (named in the video): 'Jesus entered the temple' (21:12).

## Key terms
- Hosanna: From Hebrew for save, please (Psalm 118:25); a cry of praise and plea.
- Bethphage: 'House of unripe figs,' a village on the Mount of Olives.
- Feast of Booths: Sukkot, the autumn feast when Psalm 118 was sung with waving branches.
- Court of the Gentiles: The outer court of the temple, open to the nations.
- Money changers: Traders who exchanged coins for those accepted for temple payments.
- Kingdom of priests: God's calling for His people to intercede for others (Exodus 19:6).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Psalm 118 at the feasts: Psalm 118 belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113-118), sung at the pilgrim feasts. At the Feast of Booths the Mishnah says they waved the lulav at 'Lord, please save us' (Mishnah Sukkah 3:9) and each day circled the altar saying, 'Lord, please save us. Lord, please grant us success' (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5).
- The temple's priestly families: In Jesus' day the high priesthood was appointed by Herod and then by Rome, and a few families held it. The Talmud records: 'The power of these households stemmed from the fact that the fathers were High Priests, and their sons were the Temple treasurers' (Talmud Pesachim 57a).
- The eastern gate: The gate in the eastern wall today, the Golden Gate (Gate of Mercy), was built long after Jesus and has been sealed for centuries. Jewish and later traditions connect the eastern approach with the Messiah, drawing on Zechariah 14:4 and Ezekiel 44:1-3.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "not driving chariots, like the rest of the kings, not demanding tributes, not thrusting men off, and leading about guards, but displaying His great meekness even hereby." Homilies on Matthew 66, on 21:5. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Whence it is probable this was done twice, and at different seasons." Homilies on Matthew 67, on 21:12. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- One cleansing or two? John places a temple cleansing at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2), the other Gospels at the end. Many, with Chrysostom, see two events; others think John placed one event early for theological reasons.
- Why curse a tree out of season? Mark notes 'it was not the season for figs' (Mark 11:13). Most read the act as an enacted parable of judgment, like the prophets' sign-acts, rather than a fit of hunger.
- Which mountain? Some take 'this mountain' as a general picture of the impossible; others, like the video, as the Temple Mount or the Mount of Olives in view.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- In 21:15 the LSB says 'the chief priests and the scribes' became indignant; the video calls them Pharisees there.
- The video names the high-priestly line 'Zadok or Zedekiah'; Zedekiah was Judah's last king, and the high priests of Jesus' day were appointed by Herod and by Rome rather than following Zadok's line.
- Acts 3:2 names a temple gate 'Beautiful' but does not say where it was; many place it on the inner courts rather than the outer eastern wall.
- The claims that Josephus says the chief priests owned the money exchange, and that waving palm fronds was punishable by crucifixion, are given without a source. The closest text found for the first is the Talmud's lament over the priestly houses (Pesachim 57a).
- Mark 11:17 quotes Isaiah 56:7 with 'for all the nations'; the LSB of Isaiah 56:7 reads 'for all the peoples.'
- Caption spellings: 'Bethpage' is Bethphage and 'Hosana' is Hosanna.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why did Jesus choose a donkey and colt rather than a horse or chariot?
2. What do the two crowds, from Galilee and from Jerusalem, suggest about the city's mood?
3. How does the rest of Isaiah 56 sharpen what Jesus said in the temple?
4. What does the fig tree with 'leaves only' look like in a church or a life today?
5. How is faith that 'moves this mountain' connected to praying for others?
6. Who could you intercede for this week as part of a kingdom of priests?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: Jesus expects His disciples to be a kingdom of priests that possess unwavering faith in Him and continue to intercede on behalf of God's people. The fig tree shows what happens to leaders who look fruitful but bear none. The corrupt priests were meant to draw near and intercede for God's people; now Jesus' disciples are to be His intercessors. The idea runs from Exodus 19:6 through 2 Chronicles 30:27 and Isaiah 61:6 to 1 Peter 2:5. This is not a license to ask for whatever we want, but a call to faithful, priestly prayer.
- Study note (added): write down three people or places you will pray for daily this week, and one 'leaves only' area of your own life where you want real fruit.
